lesson.title: O(n log n): Linearithmic Time, the Sweet Spot Between Linear and Quadratic
lesson.summary: An algorithm runs in linearithmic time, O(n log n), when it performs a logarithmic number of passes, each doing linear work, a pattern most famously produced by merge sort's divide and conquer strategy.
lesson.body:
Linearithmic time, written O(n log n) and pronounced roughly n log n, describes algorithms whose work is the product of a linear factor and a logarithmic factor. It sits between O(n) and O(n^2) on the growth rate spectrum: much faster than quadratic for large inputs, but not quite as fast as pure linear time. The most common way this pattern arises is an algorithm that repeatedly splits its input in half, contributing the log n part, and then does linear work at each level of splitting, contributing the n part.

Merge sort is the standard example, and it builds directly on the divide and conquer idea. It works by splitting a list in half, recursively sorting each half, and then merging the two sorted halves back together.

def merge_sort(values):
    if len(values) <= 1:
        return values
    mid = len(values) // 2
    left = merge_sort(values[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(values[mid:])
    return merge(left, right)

def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result

To see where n log n comes from, count the work level by level. Splitting a list of n elements in half repeatedly, the way merge_sort's recursion does, takes about log2(n) levels before you reach lists of size 1, the same halving pattern behind O(log n). But unlike binary search, merge sort does not discard half the data at each level, it has to merge every element back together. At each of those log2(n) levels, the merge step across all the sublists at that level does a total of about n comparisons and copies, since every element gets touched once per level. Multiply the n work per level by the log2(n) levels, and you get roughly n times log2(n) total operations, O(n log n).

The doubling thought experiment shows why O(n log n) beats O(n^2) so decisively as n grows. Suppose merge sort takes about 1 second to sort 1 million numbers, roughly 1,000,000 times log2(1,000,000), about 20, so around 20 million operations. Doubling the input to 2 million numbers gives roughly 2,000,000 times log2(2,000,000), about 21, so around 42 million operations, only about twice the work, not four times. Compare that to a quadratic O(n^2) sort like a simple bubble sort, which would roughly quadruple its operation count on the same doubling. That gap is why merge sort and other O(n log n) algorithms are the standard choice for sorting large, real world datasets, while simple O(n^2) sorts are reserved for small inputs or teaching examples.

Linearithmic time is a good reminder that Big-O classes are not always a single simple loop shape. It emerges from combining two patterns you already know, a logarithmic number of levels from repeated halving, and linear work performed at each level, which is exactly what happens whenever divide and conquer algorithms have to recombine their divided pieces.
